strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: single-reference style personalization without per-style optimization, using a fast scale-wise autoregressive backbone. The dual-stream design, Principal Feature Blending, and Structural Attention Correction form a coherent inference-time approach.

The empirical scope is reasonably substantial: 190 prompts and 10 styles, comparisons with eight personalization methods, component ablations, a 30-participant user study, and supplementary experiments varying the SVD rank and decay parameter.

The method is competitive on the reported benchmark. It obtains a harmonic score of 0.437, close to the best reported 0.438, while attaining the highest prompt-fidelity score among the compared personalization methods and a reported runtime of 3.58 seconds on an A6000.

The replacement ablation usefully illustrates the intended trade-off: full-feature replacement raises reference-image similarity but substantially harms prompt fidelity, whereas PFB plus SAC restores a better balance. The qualitative examples are diverse and generally support practical usefulness.
The supplementary qualitative results on Infinity-8B and Switti suggest that the idea may extend beyond the primary Infinity-2B configuration.
weaknesses: The central claim that the leading singular component encodes style is not adequately established. The supporting analysis operationalizes “style” almost entirely as object color, which is a semantic visual attribute rather than the artistic styles targeted by the method. Consequently, the experiment demonstrates partial color/content separation but does not validate the claimed decomposition for texture, medium, brushwork, geometry, or other style factors.

The principal quantitative style metric is CLIP similarity between the output and the complete reference image. This is confounded by reference content, as the paper itself acknowledges. Taking its harmonic mean with text similarity does not remove that confound. No dedicated leakage measurement, disentangled style representation metric, or statistically analyzed human evaluation is provided to substantiate the claimed suppression of content leakage.

The method is not fully specified for reproduction. F3 is introduced as a spatial feature tensor, but the matricization and axes used for SVD are unspecified. It is also unclear whether SAC replaces queries and keys in every transformer layer and head. Algorithm 1 applies SAC after the transformer update for a step, which would not affect that update, whereas the prose and diagram imply intervention inside the transformer. Reference preprocessing, sampling settings, seeds, and the number of samples per prompt are also omitted.

Although presented as personalization from a single reference image, the generation prompt explicitly contains a manually supplied style description, and the supplement lists a style label for every reference. The paper does not isolate how much performance comes from the image versus this style text, nor evaluate references whose style is difficult to name. This materially narrows the stated problem setting.

The efficiency comparison is misleadingly labeled as inference time: for tuning-based baselines it adds complete per-style training time to the generation of one image, while the proposed method reports generation time alone. This does not support a fair per-image latency claim, and the reported speedup is also largely attributable to the autoregressive backbone rather than the proposed modules. Matching output resolutions and other runtime settings are not documented.

The measured gain is small and lacks uncertainty estimates: the full method improves the Infinity baseline harmonic score from 0.429 to 0.437, PFB alone decreases it to 0.426, and StyleAligned slightly exceeds the full method at 0.438. No confidence intervals, repeated-seed analysis, or significance testing establishes that these differences are reliable.

The user study omits the number and selection of evaluated examples, assignments per participant, randomization, quality-control procedure, and statistical uncertainty. The generalization experiments on additional backbones are qualitative only, so the claim of model-agnostic operation remains preliminary.

Overall, the method is promising and the results are competitive, but the unsupported interpretation of color as style, confounded evaluation, incomplete technical specification, and unfair efficiency comparison are consequential rather than merely presentational. These issues currently outweigh the practical contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: single-reference style personalization without per-style optimization, using a fast scale-wise autoregressive generator rather than the more common diffusion backbone.

The proposed intervention is lightweight and practically appealing. Principal Feature Blending and Structural Attention Correction require no weight updates, and the reported 3.58-second runtime on an A6000 suggests genuine deployment potential.

The evaluation includes 190 prompts across 10 styles, eight comparison methods, component ablations, a 30-participant user study, and supplementary qualitative demonstrations on Infinity-8B and Switti. This is a broader empirical package than a purely proof-of-concept submission.

The ablation exhibits an internally consistent pattern: direct feature replacement improves image-reference similarity but substantially damages prompt fidelity; PFB recovers much of that fidelity; and SAC raises the harmonic score from 0.426 to 0.437.
The manuscript is generally readable, and the qualitative figures communicate both the intended effect and common content-leakage failure modes clearly.
weaknesses: The central interpretation that the leading singular component encodes "style" is not adequately established. The diagnostic experiment operationalizes style only as object color, using prompts such as red truck versus purple cat. Showing that the first component transfers color does not establish that it isolates the textures, strokes, geometry, or rendering characteristics represented by the artistic styles in the main benchmark. The paper extrapolates from a narrow color probe to a broad style-disentanglement claim.

The SVD mechanism is underspecified. F3 is introduced as a spatial feature tensor, but the paper does not state how it is reshaped into a matrix, which axes form U and V, whether features are centered or normalized, or whether decomposition is performed before or after quantization/upsampling. Because an uncentered leading component can largely capture global activation or color statistics, these details are consequential to both interpretation and reproducibility.

The primary quantitative evidence does not clearly demonstrate an advantage. The proposed method's harmonic score is 0.437, slightly below StyleAligned at 0.438 and only 0.003 above StyleAR, with no repeated-sampling variance, confidence intervals, or significance analysis. Moreover, CLIP image similarity to the reference is explicitly acknowledged to reward content leakage; taking its harmonic mean with text similarity does not remove that confound.

The efficiency comparison is materially misleading. Table 1 labels the quantity as inference time but adds per-style training time to the generation time of tuning-based baselines and amortizes that cost over only one output. This supports the narrow claim of lower one-shot end-to-end latency, but not a fair inference-speed comparison or the broad claim that the method is up to 195 times faster. Resolution, sampling configuration, and method-specific timing breakdowns are also not reported.

The user study is insufficiently specified to validate the perceptual claims. It reports 30 participants and forced-choice percentages, but omits the number and sampling of trials, outputs or random seeds evaluated, presentation randomization, participant allocation, raw vote counts, and uncertainty or significance tests. The study also excludes several compared methods, so it cannot substantiate superiority over the complete baseline set.

The claimed model-agnostic generalization is supported only by selected qualitative examples on Infinity-8B and Switti. There are no quantitative results, failure rates, or evidence that the same stage, decay rate, and attention intervention remain appropriate across architectures.

Important implementation details for SAC are missing, including which transformer blocks, layers, and heads receive replaced queries and keys. Its stated ordering is also ambiguous: Algorithm 1 computes each stream's new feature before applying SAC at that step, although those queries and keys would normally be used inside the transformer computation. The shift between prompt intervention at step 2, analysis of F3, and method intervention at s=3 further obscures the exact indexing.

The originality is moderate. Spectral feature decomposition/replacement and shared query-key attention both closely resemble established style-transfer and attention-sharing ideas; the main novelty is their application and empirical tailoring to the Infinity-style scale-wise autoregressive pipeline. Given the unresolved interpretation, evaluation confounds, and reproducibility gaps, the practical promise does not yet outweigh the technical weaknesses. Minor grammatical issues and mislabeled supplementary figure captions are presentation refinements and are not the basis of this rating.

strengths: The paper presents a useful training-free approach to single-reference style personalization in scale-wise autoregressive image generators. Operating without per-style optimization and producing a 1024×1024 image in a reported 3.58 seconds are practically meaningful advantages.

The proposed intervention is simple and reasonably motivated: the authors first localize an influential generation stage, then use spectrally weighted feature replacement for style injection and content-stream attention for structural preservation. The component ablation supports this division of labor: direct replacement substantially harms prompt fidelity, PFB improves the trade-off, and adding SAC raises the harmonic score from 0.426 to 0.437.

The main evaluation is favorable rather than merely benchmark-chasing. The method obtains the highest reported prompt-fidelity score (0.334), a harmonic score close to the best result (0.437 versus 0.438), and much lower reported latency. This supports the claimed practical balance even though it does not dominate every individual metric.

Qualitative comparisons and additional examples are extensive and generally convincing. They show diverse subjects and styles, visible suppression of reference-content leakage, and coherent outputs. The supplementary demonstrations on Infinity-8B and Switti provide encouraging, albeit qualitative, evidence that the mechanism is not confined to Infinity-2B.

The supplementary top-k and decay-rate experiments strengthen the proposed spectral interpretation: the first component produces the largest color-similarity change, while including more components progressively changes object structure. The hyperparameter results also indicate that performance is not highly sensitive to the selected decay rate.
The manuscript is clear and well organized, with an understandable pipeline, algorithm, implementation details, baseline sources, ablations, and a complementary human evaluation.
weaknesses: The central claim that the dominant singular component encodes “style” is supported initially using color as the style variable. Color is only one low-level attribute, and a leading singular component may naturally encode global color or intensity without representing broader artistic style. The downstream benchmark and qualitative results show practical transfer, but they do not establish the stronger general disentanglement claim.

The SVD operation is under-specified. The paper describes F3 as a spatial feature tensor but does not state how it is reshaped into a matrix, which axes form U and V, whether decomposition is performed per sample or channel, or how rank is defined. These choices materially affect the intervention and currently limit reproducibility.

The quantitative evaluation depends entirely on CLIP similarities. The authors correctly acknowledge that reference-image similarity can reward content leakage, yet the proposed harmonic mean still inherits this problem and is not independently validated as a perceptual measure. Results lack repeated-seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the 0.001 gap to the best harmonic score is therefore not meaningful evidence of superiority.

The user study is insufficiently specified for strong statistical support. Although 30 participants are reported, the number and sampling of trials per participant, output seeds, presentation randomization, tie handling, and statistical uncertainty are absent. Reporting only winner percentages makes it difficult to judge robustness or participant dependence.

The latency comparison conflates different quantities: for tuning-based methods, per-style training time is added to the generation time of a single image and labeled inference time. This strongly favors the proposed method and does not describe amortized use when many images are generated for one style. Resolution, precision, sampling settings, and batch treatment should also be reported consistently for every baseline. The efficiency advantage remains credible, but the claimed “up to 195×” comparison is not broadly representative.

The evidence for model-agnostic generalization is only qualitative on two additional backbones. Quantitative measurements of fidelity and latency, along with ablations showing whether the same intervention stage and hyperparameters remain appropriate, would be needed to substantiate the broad plug-and-play claim.

Some technical descriptions are internally imprecise: the preliminary equations define the transformer as predicting residual Rs followed by accumulation into Fs, whereas Algorithm 1 writes Fs directly as the transformer output. The algorithm also depicts SAC query/key replacement after the current feature update, although those quantities must be substituted inside the attention computation that produces the update. These appear correctable, but prevent exact implementation from the presented pseudocode.

The method incurs a dual-stream forward pass, yet computational and memory overhead relative to ordinary Infinity inference is not reported. This omission matters for the paper’s real-time and deployment-flexibility claims.
